newsitem.title: CHINA: Japan landing on disputed islands angers China.
newsitem.headline: Japan landing on disputed islands angers China.

text.p: China voiced indignation on Monday after a group of Japanese right-wing activists briefly landed on a disputed island in the East China Sea and urged Tokyo to stop such incidents from reocurring.
"We express indignation with Japanese right-wingers...for landing again on the Diaoyu islands and seriously violating China's sovereignty," Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Cui Tiankai said.
The islands, which are administered by Japan, are called the Diaoyus by China and rival Taiwan and the Senkakus by Japan.

"The Chinese Foreign Ministry has made solemn representations with the Japanese government," Cui said. "The Chinese side has asked the Japanese government...to adopt measures to prevent similar incidents from happening again in future."
Three Japanese activists, belonging to a right-wing group that erected a makeshift lighthouse on one of the islands last July, briefly landed on the island on Wednesday.
The activists inspected the lighthouse and took video footage before returning to their boat after a two-hour stay.
The landing was made despite a nearby Japanese patrol boat's call to desist.
Japan says the rocky outcrops, located midway between Taiwan and Okinawa, have been Japanese territory since 1895, while Beijing says it has owned the islets since ancient times.
The landings threaten to fan the flames of a decades-old dispute that the Japanese government is keen to play down to avoid straining ties with China.

Embarrassed Japanese leaders have said a May 6 landing by a conservative legislator who planted Japan's wartime emblem -- the Rising Sun flag -- on one of the islands was an "illegal act" that was bad for Tokyo's foreign relations.

Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto is hoping the islands dispute will not endanger a proposed exchange of visits with his Chinese counterpart Li Peng later this year to mark the 25th anniversary of bilateral ties.
Activists from Taiwan and Hong Kong sailed to the islands last month to challenge Japan's claim but were kept away by Japanese patrol ships.
